All four sampled rollouts are successful; there is no sampled failure sheet in this workspace. I’ll therefore compare the strongest rollout (`224.488` capture) against the slowest successful counterexample (`259.160` capture), while using the inherited seed’s domain-exit record only as nonvisual failure context. The three identical/repeated `244.547` results also give a useful fixed-prewarm reproducibility check.

The policy delta behind the strongest rollout is a bounded, bearing-gated body-frame lateral-velocity correction: it improves capture from `244.547` to `224.488`, lowers mean distance from `6.452L` to `6.311L`, and lowers RMS force from `18.263` to `17.943`, though mean command energy rises slightly (`695.75` to `701.39`). I’m now applying the skill’s visual check to confirm that this is productive corridor correction rather than an accidental scalar win.

The visual sheets support the metric result: the fish is self-propelled upstream (mean body velocity x `-0.04895` versus mean local-flow x `-0.03293`), enters the developed wake, and the successful path still contains a large midcourse reversal. The exact anchor repeats show an even wider loop; the heading-rate branch also loops above the target and arrives later. I’ll record a conservative exploitation hypothesis before editing: keep the proven gait and bearing/rate bundle, and increase only the already-positive away-drift lookahead from `0.08` to `0.10`, preserving its bearing gate and bounded maximum correction.

I’m now distilling the sampled result into durable guidance. The reusable lesson is narrower than “more steering helps”: the positive mechanism is sign-gated body-frame lateral velocity on top of the proven bearing/rate controller; direct heading-rate damping was a negative contrast. The boundary remains this fixed shell and wake phase, with load and effort checks required.
